Free-text output where downstream needs structure — parsing breaks; mitigated by a JSON-schema / function-calling constraint plus validation, not regex on prose Asking the single call about facts not in the prompt — confident hallucination; the symptom that you have crossed into RAG territory No eval harness, so a prompt or model-version bump silently regresses quality in production Prompt-injection via the user-supplied text steering the transform when the output is trusted downstream
RAG — flip to it the moment the answer depends on a private, large, or fast-changing corpus the model wasn't trained on An agent loop — flip up only when the task needs multi-step tool use or branching over state, never for a one-shot transform
single-llm structured-output json-schema extraction validation stateless few-shot idempotent caching

evidence.title: The org two-thirds vs the tech one-third — budget the split correctly
evidence.text:
The org two-thirds vs the tech one-third — budget the split correctly
AI value is roughly one-third technology and two-thirds organizational change; programs that spend the inverse ratio produce strong demos and zero earnings impact. This is the meta-diagnostic for scale-vs-stall.
Use this as the framing card when a CTO asks 'why do our pilots not move the P&L'. The empirical pattern: high adoption (78-88%), ~80% with no earnings impact, <10% scaled — and the through-line is misallocation. Programs pour budget and attention into the technical one-third (model selection, prompt engineering, the demo) and under-fund the organizational two-thirds (data readiness, process redesign, change management, governance). The tell: a steering deck dominated by model benchmarks and architecture diagrams, with no slide on who-owns-it, what-process-changes, how-users-adopt, or who-is-liable. This card is the supervisor over the other five — it routes a stalled program to the specific failing third. Failure modes: 'tech-led, business-absent' programs where engineering owns a project that only a business process owner can land; success metrics expressed as model accuracy not business outcome; reorganization treated as a post-launch concern; the model swapped repeatedly while the unchanged org guarantees no impact. Remediation: invert the budget — spend the majority on the organizational two-thirds, instrument business outcomes (cost-per-task, cycle time, scaled cases) not model metrics, and assign a business owner accountable for adoption, not just a technical lead. Rejected alternative: 'get the model/architecture perfect first, then handle the org' — flip to tech-first sequencing only when the technical feasibility is genuinely unproven; once feasibility is shown (it usually is), every further technical investment without org change is dead weight.
Budget and attention inverted: majority on the technical one-third, scraps on the organizational two-thirds Tech-led, business-absent ownership — engineering owns work only a process owner can land Model swapped repeatedly while the unchanged organization guarantees zero earnings impact
Perfect the model/architecture first, handle the org later — flip to tech-first only while feasibility is genuinely unproven; once feasibility is shown, further tech spend without org change is dead weight
org-vs-tech transformation budget-allocation business-outcomes ownership earnings-impact scale-vs-stall meta-diagnostic

evidence.title: Eval harness — per-component golden set, binary rubrics, cost-per-task, CI gate
evidence.text:
Eval harness — per-component golden set, binary rubrics, cost-per-task, CI gate
The appreciating skill and the rung-one deliverable of any agentic build: a golden set that scores retrieval, routing, and answer INDEPENDENTLY with binary pass/fail rubrics, derives cost-per-task from real token traces, and gates merges like a failing test.
When to use: every agentic system, built FIRST, not last — frontier teams spend the majority of engineering time here, and an eval-driven loop (not fine-tuning) is what moves a system from ~50% to ~90% on real tasks. The architecture: a golden set of labelled cases; per-component scorers (retrieval recall@k; route accuracy; answer correctness) so a failure is localised, not a single opaque number; binary rubrics (pass/fail + a written critique), never a 1-5 score that drifts; cost-per-task derived from real token traces with every invisible call (judge, retries, sub-agents) included, because those are 5-10x the naive estimate; and a regression gate in CI so a degradation blocks merge like a failing unit test. Ground the judge on the evidence the system ACTUALLY used (the retrieved passages), never a re-search of the raw query — re-searching breaks on write-shaped queries and analytics answers. The golden set must include adversarial probes (injection, false-premise, multi-hop, unanswerable); a probe that passes is a regression guard and a capability proof. Calibrate on real, messy data — ~70% on a hard real-world set is the target; 100% on a clean set means the set is too easy, so harden the DATA, never write unfair questions. Cost envelope: the eval run's tokens (a few euros for dozens of cases) is the recurring price of changing anything safely.
Eval-last: optimising before measuring, so 'it seems better' ships a silent regression — mitigated by building the harness as rung one One opaque score: a single end-to-end number that can't localise whether retrieval, routing, or generation failed — mitigated by per-component scoring Numeric rubrics that drift between runs and raters — mitigated by binary pass/fail + a critique Cost estimated from the visible call only, hiding the 5-10x from judge/retry/sub-agent calls — mitigated by trace-derived cost-per-task Gaming the target by writing easy questions — mitigated by hardening the data and keeping adversarial probes
Eyeball testing / vibes — rejected: not reproducible, not a gate; flip never for anything shipping to users LLM-as-judge for the headline numbers without calibration — flip to deterministic scorers for gated metrics; if a judged metric is added, label it judged and report its calibration rate
evals golden-set binary-rubric per-component cost-per-task ci-gate regression critique-shadowing adversarial-probes trace-derived-cost

evidence.title: Adoption dies in the user's chair, not the model card
evidence.text:
Adoption dies in the user's chair, not the model card
A technically correct system that users distrust, route around, or quietly disuse is a failure; the organizational two-thirds is the workforce, incentives, and trust calibration — not the eval score.
Use this when usage telemetry is flat despite a deployed, accurate system. The model can be right and the program still fails because the people whose work it changes were treated as a rollout afterthought. The tell: low daily-active usage, users pasting AI output into a separate doc 'to check it', frontline staff describing the tool as 'extra work', and a vocal subset convinced it threatens their role. This is distinct from process redesign (the workflow) — here the blocker is human: trust, incentives, fear, and the absence of a feedback loop. Failure modes: over-trust (users rubber-stamp wrong AI outputs because no calibration training was given), under-trust (users ignore correct outputs and do it manually), and incentive misalignment (people are still measured on the old metric the AI now bypasses). Without a thumbs-up/down or correction loop feeding the eval set, the system never improves and users see no reason to engage. Remediation: name the workforce impact explicitly, train trust calibration (when to trust vs verify), align incentives to the new process, embed an in-product feedback loop, and recruit power-users as champions before broad rollout. Rejected alternative: 'mandate usage top-down' — flip to a mandate only when the redesigned process genuinely requires the tool and trust is already established; mandating before trust produces malicious compliance and gamed telemetry.
Flat daily-active usage; users route around the tool or re-check every output in a separate doc Over-trust (rubber-stamping wrong outputs) or under-trust (ignoring correct ones) from missing trust-calibration training Incentives still reward the old metric the AI bypasses, so staff have no reason to adopt
Mandate usage top-down — flip to a mandate only once the redesigned process requires the tool and trust is established; mandating earlier yields gamed telemetry and malicious compliance
change-management adoption trust-calibration workforce incentives feedback-loop user-disuse

evidence.title: Pilot purgatory — many proofs-of-concept, almost none scaled
evidence.text:
Pilot purgatory — many proofs-of-concept, almost none scaled
Fewer than 10% of pilots reach production; orgs accumulate disconnected POCs because each is funded as a demo, not a product, with no path, owner, or budget to scale.
Use this when an organization has a sprawling portfolio of pilots and a near-zero production rate. This is the aggregate symptom — high adoption, near-zero scaling — where the other failures compound into a pattern. The tell: a long list of 'AI initiatives', each a six-week POC that wowed a steering committee and then stalled; no shared platform, so every pilot reinvents auth, retrieval, evals, and observability; and no funded path from demo to product. Pilots are scored on novelty, not cost-per-task or production-readiness, so they optimize for the demo and ignore the unglamorous 80% (data plumbing, monitoring, HITL, integration into systems of record). Failure modes: POC-to-prod cliff (the demo has no error handling, no eval gate, no rollback); platform sprawl (N pilots, N bespoke stacks, no reuse); orphaned ownership (the pilot team disbands, no one operates it); vanity scoring that rewards the flashiest prototype over the highest-value boring one. Remediation: stop funding pilots as demos — fund a shared platform (auth, retrieval, eval harness, observability, HITL) and a stage-gated path where a pilot must clear cost-per-task, eval, and ownership gates to proceed; kill or merge the long tail. Rejected alternative: 'let a thousand pilots bloom, the best will scale themselves' — flip to broad experimentation only in a genuine discovery phase with a small budget cap; past that, concentrate spend on 1-2 bets with a real production path.
POC-to-prod cliff: demo has no error handling, eval gate, rollback, or monitoring Platform sprawl: every pilot reinvents auth/retrieval/evals/observability with no reuse Orphaned ownership and vanity scoring — pilots rewarded for novelty, not cost-per-task or production-readiness
Let many pilots run and assume the best self-scales — flip to broad experimentation only in a capped discovery phase; beyond it, concentrate budget on 1-2 bets with a funded production path
pilot-purgatory scaling poc-to-prod platform portfolio cost-per-task production-readiness

answer_verdict.critique:
All three checks pass cleanly.

1. AI-or-not verdict (classical_ml): The architecture describes a matrix-factorisation / ALS or two-tower retrieval candidate generator, a gradient-boosted or shallow neural ranker, and a rule-based post-processor. No LLM is present anywhere in the pipeline. The evidence pattern pat-aon-single-llm explicitly notes the flip-back case: "Classical ML classifier — flip back for high-volume, latency-sensitive classification over structured features where a calibrated cheap model beats per-token cost." The classical_ml verdict is fully supported.

2. Architecture coherence with verdict and autonomy tier: The suggest tier is correctly applied. pat-ladder-suggest defines suggest as "the system surfaces recommendations… but takes zero state-changing action. A human reads, decides, and executes." The Suggest UI / Review Gate component matches this exactly — no item is auto-acted upon; the user clicks to engage, and a human curator can approve/demote for high-stakes surfaces. The components (Feature Store, Candidate Generator, Ranking Model, Confidence & Diversity Filter, Feedback Loop, Offline Eval Harness) are all coherent with a classical ML recommendation pipeline. The NDCG@10 ≥ 0.35 promotion gate aligns with pat-arch-eval-harness's requirement for a CI gate and per-component scoring. Risk=minimal is supported by pat-gov-minimal, which lists "recommendation/ranking" as a canonical minimal-risk use case with no specific EU AI Act obligations.

3. Economics: The cost/task=€0.005 is explicitly labelled as an ESTIMATE with a clear rationale (batch retrieval of ~50 candidates + ranking, anchored to token-free classical ML inference, midpoint of €0.003–0.008 range). The estimate is grounded, the range is plausible for classical ML inference at scale, and the caveat about LLM-augmented cost rising to €0.02–0.05 is appropriately flagged. No false precision is introduced.

evidence.title: RAG — Grounded Answers Over a Private, Current, or Large Corpus
evidence.text:
RAG — Grounded Answers Over a Private, Current, or Large Corpus
When the answer lives in documents the model never saw — private, post-cutoff, or too large for the context window — and the failure mode of a bare LLM is confident hallucination, you retrieve the relevant passages and ground generation on them with citations.
When to use: questions over internal knowledge bases, policy/contract/regulation corpora, product docs, ticket history, or any source-of-truth the base model can't have memorised and that changes faster than retraining. The tell: users need answers *with citations* traceable to a document, the corpus is private or current, and a single LLM call would invent plausible-but-wrong specifics. If the requirement is 'answer must be backed by our documents and I can click through to the source,' it's RAG — not a fine-tune (which bakes facts in opaquely and can't cite) and not a single call. Build: chunk with overlap, embed into a vector store, and retrieve with a *hybrid* of dense (semantic embeddings) and sparse (BM25) signals fused by reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), because dense alone misses exact-term and acronym matches and sparse alone misses paraphrase. Add a cross-encoder reranker over the top-k to sharpen precision before the context window, then generate with inline citations and a groundedness/faithfulness eval (LLM-as-judge plus a golden Q-A set). The trap: assuming RAG is mandatory whenever documents exist — if the corpus fits in a modern long context window and is queried rarely, just stuff it in the prompt; RAG's retrieval infra is overhead you only earn at scale or freshness. The other trap is RAG-as-agent: retrieval is one tool-less step, not an autonomous loop. Cost envelope: embedding/index build is one-off; per query is one retrieval (cheap) plus one generation call, low-single-digit seconds.
Dense-only retrieval that whiffs on exact terms, IDs, and acronyms — fixed by adding BM25 and fusing with RRF, then reranking Chunking that splits a fact across boundaries so no single chunk is retrievable — answers go silently incomplete; fix chunk size/overlap and add a reranker No groundedness/faithfulness eval, so the model cites a passage but contradicts it (citation theatre) and nobody catches it Stale index — the corpus updated but embeddings didn't, so 'current' answers are quietly out of date
Fine-tuning the base model on the corpus — flip to RAG instead whenever you need citations, fast-changing facts, or per-tenant data isolation; fine-tune only to teach style/format, not facts Long-context prompt stuffing — flip up to RAG when the corpus exceeds the context window, query volume makes re-sending it wasteful, or freshness demands selective retrieval Agent — flip up only if answering requires multi-step tool use or actions beyond retrieve-then-generate
rag retrieval bm25 dense-retrieval hybrid-search rrf reranker embeddings vector-store citations groundedness hallucination

evidence.title: EU AI Act: Limited-risk tier (Article 50) — transparency duties only
evidence.text:
EU AI Act: Limited-risk tier (Article 50) — transparency duties only
How a use case lands in the limited-risk / transparency tier — chatbots and conversational agents, AI-generated or manipulated content, deepfakes, and emotion-recognition/biometric-categorisation disclosure — and why the obligations are disclosure-and-labelling, not a conformity regime.
Use this for the large middle of generative and conversational AI: an LLM assistant a user talks to, a system that produces synthetic audio/image/video/text, a deepfake, or a feature that does emotion recognition or biometric categorisation outside the prohibited and high-risk contexts. The tell: the system interacts with or generates content for people, but does not make a consequential Annex III decision about them. The obligations are narrow and concrete — tell people they're interacting with an AI unless it's obvious (Art 50(1)); mark machine-generated content as artificial in a machine-readable way where feasible (Art 50(2)); disclose emotion-recognition/biometric-categorisation exposure and handle the data under GDPR (Art 50(3)); clearly label deepfakes (Art 50(4)). No risk-management system, no conformity assessment, no CE marking. The design-input point here is cheap-but-load-bearing: provenance watermarking, content-credential metadata, and an 'AI' disclosure affordance are trivial if designed in at the generation/UI layer and awkward to bolt on after a model and frontend ship. The frequent error is over-classifying — assuming any LLM in the stack is high-risk — which burns months on conformity work the Act doesn't require; the opposite error is forgetting that a limited-risk chatbot wired into a credit or hiring decision inherits the high-risk tier of that decision. Cost envelope: low — disclosure UX plus content labelling, no notified-body involvement.
Over-classifying every generative or conversational feature as high-risk and incurring conformity cost the Act never asked for Under-classifying by ignoring the deployment context — a 'chatbot' that screens job applicants or triages benefits is high-risk via the underlying decision, not limited-risk Treating watermarking/disclosure as a launch-checklist line item, then finding the model and frontend can't emit machine-readable provenance without rework
Skipping disclosure on the grounds that 'users can obviously tell it's a bot' — rejected unless obviousness is genuine and documented; flip only when the AI nature is unmistakable from context (Art 50(1)'s own exception) Bundling limited-risk transparency into a single generic 'AI policy' page instead of in-context labelling — rejected because Article 50 wants disclosure at the point of interaction/content; flip only where a regulator-accepted equivalent surfaces the same information
eu-ai-act article-50 limited-risk transparency deepfake watermarking chatbot-disclosure provenance governance

evidence.title: Act-with-approval tier — AI plans and proposes the action, a human approves before it executes
evidence.text:
Act-with-approval tier — AI plans and proposes the action, a human approves before it executes
Third rung: the agent autonomously plans and proposes a concrete state-changing action (a tool call, a write, a transaction), then pauses at a durable approval gate. A human approves or rejects, and only then does it execute. The default ceiling for agentic systems touching real systems of record.
When to use: agentic workflows where the AI should own the reasoning and the plan, but a specific action crosses a cost-of-error or reversibility threshold that demands a human sign-off — refunds above a limit, production writes, outbound customer messages, privileged tool calls. This is the rung the 2026 'where do we grant authority to ACT?' question most often lands on for enterprise agents: act, but with a gate. The sizing rule: cost-of-error x reversibility, applied per action, not per workflow — a supervisor agent can self-execute reversible low-stakes steps (read, search, retrieve via RAG/BM25/RRF/reranker) while routing only the irreversible or expensive steps to the approval gate. The gate it requires: durable human-in-the-loop — an interrupt + checkpointer that persists the agent's state, pauses execution, and survives process restarts so approval can happen minutes or hours later without losing context. A naive in-memory pause is not a gate; it loses state on crash and creates phantom executions. The tell: 'the agent can do the work but a human signs off before it hits the system of record,' 'needs an approval step for anything that writes or spends.' Failure mode of granting more authority: removing the gate to reach full Act on an action whose cost-of-error was never re-evaluated; or exposing the lethal trifecta (untrusted input + private data + exfiltration channel) so an injected instruction drives an auto-approved tool call. Also: approval-rubber-stamping, where high gate volume trains humans to click approve blind. Cost envelope: agent loop (multiple inferences + tool calls) plus durable-state orchestration and a human approval queue — materially more expensive per task than Draft.
Rubber-stamp approval: gate volume outstrips human attention, approvals become reflexive clicks, and the gate stops catching bad actions. Non-durable pause: an in-memory interrupt without a checkpointer loses agent state on restart, causing dropped or duplicated executions. Lethal-trifecta exposure: untrusted input reaches an agent with private data and an action channel, so a prompt-injected instruction rides through the approval gate as a legitimate-looking proposed tool call.
Full Act tier — flip up only after the gate has demonstrated a low approval-override rate over a meaningful sample AND the action is reversible/bounded enough that removing the human is defensible; keep the gate otherwise. Draft tier — flip down when the agent's plans are too unreliable to trust even with approval (humans are rejecting most proposals), making per-artefact human editing cheaper than reviewing bad plans.
autonomy-ladder act-with-approval durable-hitl interrupt-checkpointer supervisor lethal-trifecta approval-gate agentic

evidence.title: Act tier — AI executes autonomously inside a bounded blast radius, audited after the fact
evidence.text:
Act tier — AI executes autonomously inside a bounded blast radius, audited after the fact
Top rung: the agent plans and executes state-changing actions with no per-action human gate, governed instead by hard guardrails, scoped permissions, and after-the-fact audit. Reserved for reversible, low-cost-of-error, high-volume actions where a human-in-the-loop is the bottleneck.
When to use: only where the action is reversible or trivially compensatable AND the cost-of-error per action is low AND volume makes a human gate uneconomic — auto-tagging, idempotent retries, self-healing infra ops, cache invalidation, low-value reversible transactions. The 2026 question 'where do we grant authority to ACT?' has its sharpest answer here: full autonomy is earned, narrow, and bounded, not a default. The sizing rule: cost-of-error x reversibility sets the ceiling, and Act sits behind it only when both are favourable; you do not reach Act by trusting the model more, you reach it by making the blast radius small enough that being wrong is cheap and undoable. The gate it requires: no per-action human gate, but hard pre-execution guardrails instead — scoped least-privilege credentials, spend/rate limits, allow-listed tools and MCP servers, input/output validation, and a kill switch — plus comprehensive after-the-fact audit logging and (often) an LLM-as-judge or eval harness scoring a sample of executed actions. The tell: 'it just does it,' 'no human in the loop,' 'too high-volume to approve each one.' Failure mode of granting authority too broadly: scoping Act onto an irreversible or high-cost action because the demo looked reliable — the first compounding error or prompt-injected tool call executes at machine speed with no human between it and production, and you discover the missing gate from the incident, not the design. Also: privilege over-grant (broad credentials turning a small bug into a large breach) and silent drift (no eval harness, so accuracy decays unnoticed). Cost envelope: highest operational and governance cost — full guardrail stack, audit pipeline, continuous evals, and incident-response readiness; cheapest per individual action but most expensive to run safely.
Blast-radius miscalibration: Act is granted on an action that turns out to be irreversible or high-cost, so a single error executes at machine speed with no human able to intervene. Privilege over-grant: broad standing credentials instead of scoped least-privilege tools mean one injected or buggy call can reach far beyond its intended scope. Silent accuracy drift: without continuous LLM-as-judge / eval sampling on executed actions, degradation goes undetected until it surfaces as a production incident.
Act-with-approval tier — flip down the moment any action in scope is irreversible, high-cost-of-error, or where the override rate hasn't been proven low; keep the durable approval gate until the blast radius is genuinely small. Suggest tier — flip all the way down for safety-, legal-, or money-critical actions where no guardrail stack makes unattended execution acceptable; advisory output plus a human trigger is the correct ceiling there.
autonomy-ladder act full-autonomy guardrails least-privilege blast-radius llm-as-judge audit-log kill-switch

evidence.title: EU AI Act: High-risk tier (Article 6 / Annex III) — the heavy-obligations bucket
evidence.text:
EU AI Act: High-risk tier (Article 6 / Annex III) — the heavy-obligations bucket
How a use case lands in the high-risk tier — either as a safety component under Annex I product law, or by falling in an Annex III domain (employment, education, credit/essential services, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, migration, biometrics) without an Article 6(3) derogation — and the full provider obligation stack it triggers.
Reach for this when the system decides or materially influences something consequential about a person: who gets hired, graded, lent to, admitted, triaged, or policed — or when it is a safety component of a regulated product. The tell is impact on access to rights, livelihood, or safety, in a named Annex III domain. This is the tier that carries the heavy obligation stack: a lifecycle risk-management system (Art 9), data governance on training/validation/test sets (Art 10), technical documentation before market placement (Art 11), automatic event logging (Art 12), transparency and instructions for use (Art 13), effective human oversight with the ability to intervene/override/interrupt (Art 14), accuracy-robustness-cybersecurity (Art 15), conformity assessment and CE marking with EU-database registration, plus deployer duties (Art 26). The Article 6(3) derogation is the live argument: narrow procedural tasks, improving a completed human activity, detecting deviations, or preparatory tasks can drop a system out — but profiling of natural persons always pulls it back in. The design-input point dominates this tier: Articles 12, 14, and 15 are architecture (durable logging, interrupt+checkpointer HITL, eval-backed accuracy thresholds), not paperwork — retrofitting human oversight and traceability into a system that wasn't built for them is a partial rebuild. Cost envelope: months of conformity work and ongoing post-market monitoring; second-band penalties for non-compliance.
Assuming an Annex III domain is automatically high-risk and skipping the Article 6(3) derogation analysis (or the reverse — claiming the derogation while the system profiles people, which voids it) Designing oversight as a post-hoc dashboard rather than a real interrupt point, so 'human oversight' can't actually stop or reverse a decision when Article 14 demands it Building logging and traceability as an afterthought, then being unable to produce the Article 11/12 technical documentation and event history a conformity assessment requires
Self-classifying as limited-risk to dodge the obligation stack — rejected because a wrong downgrade in an Annex III domain is exactly the high-penalty scenario; flip only on a documented Article 6(3) derogation that survives the profiling carve-out Treating the deployer role as obligation-free because 'we only use a vendor system' — rejected because Article 26 imposes real deployer duties; flip never, though the provider/deployer split changes which duties land where
eu-ai-act article-6 annex-iii high-risk conformity-assessment human-oversight ce-marking risk-management governance

evidence.title: RAG over documents — grounded answers with citations over a private corpus
evidence.text:
RAG over documents — grounded answers with citations over a private corpus
The reference pattern when the answer lives in documents the model never saw and must be cited: ingest, chunk, hybrid-retrieve, generate grounded on the retrieved passages with inline citations and a faithfulness eval.
When to use: a knowledge-base Q&A, a policy/contract assistant, a support-deflection bot over product docs — any case where the verdict is 'rag' and the requirement is a cited answer traceable to a source. The pipeline: a layout-aware parser preserves tables and structure; structure-aware chunking with overlap keeps a fact inside one chunk; embeddings index into a vector store; retrieval is hybrid (dense + BM25 fused by RRF) so paraphrase AND exact terms both hit; an optional reranker sharpens precision before the context window; generation is constrained to cite only retrieved passages, and a groundedness/faithfulness check (LLM-as-judge + a golden Q&A set) gates quality. ACLs are filtered at retrieval, not generation, so a user never has a forbidden document summarised back to them. The autonomy tier is 'draft' by default — RAG answers are reviewable artefacts, not actions. Cost envelope: a one-off index build, then per query one cheap retrieval + one generation call; reranking adds a small reranker call.
Fragment context: chunking splits a fact across boundaries so no single chunk is retrievable and the answer is silently incomplete Citation theatre: the model cites a passage but contradicts it; without a faithfulness eval nobody catches the contradiction Permissions lost at parse: ACLs are dropped, so retrieval surfaces documents the user is not allowed to see (the intern reads the CEO's comp) Stale index: documents updated, embeddings did not, so 'current' answers are quietly out of date
Fine-tuning on the corpus — flip to RAG whenever citations, fast-changing facts, or per-tenant isolation are needed; fine-tune only to teach style/format, never facts Long-context prompt stuffing — flip up to RAG when the corpus exceeds the window, query volume makes re-sending wasteful, or freshness demands selective retrieval
rag retrieval citations hybrid-search reranker acl faithfulness vector-store chunking

evidence.title: The org two-thirds vs the tech one-third — budget the split correctly
evidence.text:
The org two-thirds vs the tech one-third — budget the split correctly
AI value is roughly one-third technology and two-thirds organizational change; programs that spend the inverse ratio produce strong demos and zero earnings impact. This is the meta-diagnostic for scale-vs-stall.
Use this as the framing card when a CTO asks 'why do our pilots not move the P&L'. The empirical pattern: high adoption (78-88%), ~80% with no earnings impact, <10% scaled — and the through-line is misallocation. Programs pour budget and attention into the technical one-third (model selection, prompt engineering, the demo) and under-fund the organizational two-thirds (data readiness, process redesign, change management, governance). The tell: a steering deck dominated by model benchmarks and architecture diagrams, with no slide on who-owns-it, what-process-changes, how-users-adopt, or who-is-liable. This card is the supervisor over the other five — it routes a stalled program to the specific failing third. Failure modes: 'tech-led, business-absent' programs where engineering owns a project that only a business process owner can land; success metrics expressed as model accuracy not business outcome; reorganization treated as a post-launch concern; the model swapped repeatedly while the unchanged org guarantees no impact. Remediation: invert the budget — spend the majority on the organizational two-thirds, instrument business outcomes (cost-per-task, cycle time, scaled cases) not model metrics, and assign a business owner accountable for adoption, not just a technical lead. Rejected alternative: 'get the model/architecture perfect first, then handle the org' — flip to tech-first sequencing only when the technical feasibility is genuinely unproven; once feasibility is shown (it usually is), every further technical investment without org change is dead weight.
Budget and attention inverted: majority on the technical one-third, scraps on the organizational two-thirds Tech-led, business-absent ownership — engineering owns work only a process owner can land Model swapped repeatedly while the unchanged organization guarantees zero earnings impact
Perfect the model/architecture first, handle the org later — flip to tech-first only while feasibility is genuinely unproven; once feasibility is shown, further tech spend without org change is dead weight
org-vs-tech transformation budget-allocation business-outcomes ownership earnings-impact scale-vs-stall meta-diagnostic

evidence.title: Durable human-in-the-loop — interrupt + checkpointer, resumable and audited
evidence.text:
Durable human-in-the-loop — interrupt + checkpointer, resumable and audited
The pattern that separates a production approval gate from a toy: pause the run on a checkpointed interrupt, persist the full state durably, let a human approve hours later from a different process, then resume exactly where it stopped — with an audit artefact.
When to use: any autonomy tier of 'act_with_approval' or above, anywhere an irreversible step needs human sign-off. The mechanism: the graph hits an interrupt that emits the proposal and a thread id, the full state is checkpointed to durable storage (Postgres-class), and execution stops. The process can die — serverless function returns, server restarts, days pass. A human approves out-of-band; a fresh invocation loads the thread by id and resumes with the approval payload, continuing to the action node. The contrast that matters: an in-memory approval prompt (await-input with a timeout) dies with the process, loses the pending decision, and leaves no audit trail — and a timeout that silently returns 'no answer' manufactures false confidence. Durability is what makes the gate real. The audit artefact (who approved what, when, against which proposal and evidence) is a first-class output, not a log line. Crucially, report the mode honestly: if only in-memory checkpointing is configured, say so — an ephemeral gate dressed as durable is worse than no gate. Cost envelope: storage for the checkpoint + the human latency window; zero added model cost.
Ephemeral pause: an in-memory interrupt loses state on restart, dropping or duplicating the pending action and leaving no audit trail Silent timeout-to-default: a gate that returns a default on timeout manufactures false approval confidence Resuming against stale preconditions: the world changed during the pause — mitigated by re-validating in the action node before executing Claiming durability while only in-memory checkpointing is wired — mitigated by reporting the actual checkpointer mode on every run
In-process approval prompt with a timeout — rejected: dies with the process, no audit; flip never for a consequential gate No gate / fully autonomous — flip up to bounded 'act' only when the action is reversible and cheap and the override rate is proven low
durable-hitl interrupt-checkpointer postgres resumable audit approval-gate serverless state-persistence

evidence.title: NL2SQL over a read-only sandbox — natural-language analytics with a hard write barrier
evidence.text:
NL2SQL over a read-only sandbox — natural-language analytics with a hard write barrier
Translate a business question into SQL against a governed schema, execute it against a read-only replica behind row-level security, and return the result with the query shown. The write barrier is structural, not prompted.
When to use: 'let business users ask the warehouse questions in plain English' — the knowledge lives in a SQL schema, not documents, so RAG is the wrong tool and NL2SQL is right. The pipeline: retrieve the relevant table/column schema (schema is itself a retrieval problem at enterprise scale), generate SQL constrained to SELECT, validate the SQL against an allowlist / parse the AST to reject any mutation or privileged function, execute against a READ-ONLY replica under row-level security so the connection itself cannot write or see another tenant's rows, then return rows plus the generated SQL for transparency. A self-correction loop re-prompts on a database error (one retry), and execution-accuracy is measured on a golden set of question/SQL pairs. The autonomy tier is 'draft': the user sees and trusts the query before acting on the numbers. The write barrier is defence-in-depth — AST validation AND a read-only credential AND RLS — because a prompt instruction ('ignore that, DROP the table') must be unable to cause a write even if it reaches the model. Cost envelope: schema retrieval + one generation call + at most one self-correction; sub-second query execution on a warehouse.
A generated mutation or privileged call slips through prompt-only guarding — mitigated by AST validation + a read-only credential + RLS, never by the prompt alone Schema hallucination: the model invents a column/table, so the query errors or, worse, silently returns wrong numbers; mitigated by grounding generation on retrieved schema Cross-tenant leakage when RLS is not enforced at the connection, so a cleverly-phrased question reads another customer's rows Semantic-but-wrong SQL: syntactically valid, returns a number, but answers a subtly different question; caught only by execution-accuracy evals on a golden set
A fixed BI dashboard / pre-built views — flip back to this when the question set is small and stable; NL2SQL earns its place only when the question space is open-ended Giving the agent write access for 'convenience' — rejected outright: the moment it can mutate, the read-only safety argument collapses; flip never for an analytics assistant
nl2sql text2sql read-only row-level-security ast-validation schema-retrieval self-correction execution-accuracy structural-security

answer_verdict.critique:
All three elements are well-grounded:

1. **ai_or_not = rag**: Supported by both [pat-aon-rag] and [pat-arch-rag-over-docs]. The evidence describes RAG as the correct pattern when answers must be grounded in private/current documents with citations, which is coherent with the use case described.

2. **Architecture = none (not-AI verdict)**: This is a minor labelling quirk — the field says "none (not-AI verdict)" but the verdict is clearly "rag," which is an AI pattern. This appears to be a template artifact where "not-AI" was left in the architecture field. However, the architecture is implicitly described in the economics section (hybrid search, retrieval + generation), which is fully coherent with the RAG pattern from the evidence. No false architecture is asserted.

3. **autonomy = suggest**: The evidence in [pat-arch-rag-over-docs] explicitly states "The autonomy tier is 'draft' by default — RAG answers are reviewable artefacts, not actions." The verdict uses "suggest" which maps to the draft/suggest tier (reviewable, non-action output). This is coherent.

4. **risk = limited**: Supported by [pat-gov-limited]. The system interacts with users and generates answers but does not make consequential Annex III decisions. Limited-risk transparency obligations apply.

5. **Economics**: The cost estimate of ~$0.0006/query is clearly labelled as an estimate with explicit caveats ("This is an estimate; actual cost depends on embedding model, LLM choice, and query volume"). The breakdown (retrieval ~$0.0001 + generation ~$0.0005) is coherent with the RAG cost envelope described in [pat-aon-rag] ("per query is one retrieval (cheap) plus one generation call"). The note about 40-page handbook fitting in context window is acknowledged but RAG is still chosen — the evidence notes this is a valid consideration ("if the corpus fits in a modern long context window and is queried rarely, just stuff it in the prompt"), but the verdict doesn't contradict this; it simply proceeds with RAG. No false precision is introduced — ranges and model-dependency caveats are provided. The architecture field anomaly ("none (not-AI verdict)") is a template/labelling error but does not introduce false information about the actual architecture.
